title: Vijayadashami: Rama's lotus for Durga
hookLine: before fighting Ravana, Rama offers Durga 108 lotuses, and one is missing
carry: shakti: even rama bowed to the goddess first
tomorrow: Bali Pratipada: the demon king welcomed home
last: GANESHA COUNTS THE LOVE, NOT THE FEAST.

cards: On the same autumn day, in three corners of India, three different things are happening. In a Delhi park, a crowd watches a giant paper-and-bamboo Ravana as someone fires a flaming arrow into it.

In Kolkata, married women smear red sindoor on each other's faces, laughing and crying, before an image of Durga about to leave for the river. In a Kerala home, a small child writes their first letters in a plate of rice.
It's all one day: the tenth.

teach.b: The tenth day after the nine nights is Vijayadashami, the victory tenth. In much of North India it's Dussehra, and it belongs to Rama: many towns stage the Ramlila for nine nights, and on the tenth, Ravana burns.
In Bengal it's the last day of Durga Puja, when women smear sindoor on each other before the Goddess goes to the river.

teach.h: WHY RAMA AND DURGA SHARE A DAY.
teach.b: So why do Rama and Durga share a day? Bengal's own Ramayana, by the poet Krittivas, tells a story Valmiki doesn't. Before the last battle with Ravana, Rama worships the Goddess, out of season, in autumn.
He needs a hundred and eight blue lotuses, and Hanuman brings them.

teach.h: ONE MISSING. HE OFFERS HIS EYE.
teach.b: But at the last offering, one lotus is missing: the Goddess has hidden it, to test him. Rama remembers that people call his eyes lotus-like. He lifts an arrow to offer one of his own eyes.
And Durga appears, stops his hand, and blesses him with victory. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: SHAKTI: THE POWER BEHIND THE VICTORY.
teach.b: In Hinduism the Goddess is Shakti, the power behind every victory, even a god's.

teach.h: EVEN RAMA BOWED TO THE GODDESS FIRST.
teach.b: Rama, Vishnu come down, still bows to her before he fights. So many families treat the victory tenth as the best day to begin.
The day before, much of the South honors tools and books on Ayudha Puja; on the tenth, in Kerala, many small children write their first letters in rice, an elder guiding their finger.
You start something with her blessing, because the strength to finish it is hers.

how: Navaratri ends on Vijayadashami: many North Indian towns stage the Ramlila and burn Ravana's effigy on Dussehra; in Bengal, Durga's image is immersed after sindoor khela; in much of the South, families honor tools and books on Ayudha Puja, the ninth day, and on the tenth many children begin learning to write.

o: a festival of lamps for the new moon in autumn
a nine-day pilgrimage to the source of the Ganga
nine nights that end in the tenth day's victories

games.q: the victory tenth — tap the pairs.

s: vijaya, victory, and dashami, the tenth day.
in Bengal's Ramayana, Rama worships Durga before his last battle
the poet Krittivas tells of 108 lotuses, one hidden by the Goddess to test him.
Valmiki's Ramayana tells of Rama offering Durga 108 lotuses
it's Bengal's Ramayana, by the poet Krittivas, that tells it.

games.q: you're Rama. a hundred and seven lotuses offered, and the last one is gone. what do you do?
o: stop the worship; a hundred and seven is close enough.
offer one of your own lotus-like eyes.
games.why: in Krittivas's telling, he lifts an arrow to his eye, and Durga stops him and blesses him with victory.

practice: Place in front of you, or picture, one tool you use every day: a pen, a phone, your own hands. Look at it the way people on Ayudha Puja do, with thanks. Then name one thing you're about to begin.

If you pray, ask the Goddess, as Durga or Saraswati or simply Ma, for the strength to see it through. If you don't pray, take one slow breath before you start, the way Rama paused to bow before he fought.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess that end on Vijayadashami: Ravana burned in the North, Durga's farewell in Bengal, first letters in the South, and all of it her strength.

orig.note: Sanskrit vijaya (victory) + daśamī (the tenth lunar day).

carryVoice: Your line: shakti, even Rama bowed to the Goddess first. A child's first letter counts as a victory too. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.
